results.best_explanation: E - Exit  P - Peptidyl  A - Aminoacyl Ribosomes are composed of three major sites: the entry site (or peptidyl site), the Aminoacyl site and the Exit site.  The peptidyl site is the location of peptidyl bonds being formed. The Aminoacyl site is the location of the new tRNA being charged with an amino acid. The Exit site is the site of peptidyl site and the Aminoacyl site. In translocation, the tRNA at the Aminoacyl site is released and moves towards the Exit site. Once the tRNA at the Peptidyl site reaches the Aminoacyl site, peptidyl site is available for the next cycle. results.question: Given question: Colin the cell is still on his quest to have a family. The production of his protein has now entered into the translation phase. Every protein starts with a methionine amino acid. The codon that codes for this is AUG. What anticodon would the complementary tRNA molecule possess? Option A: TAC Option B: GCA Option C: CGU Option D: CGT Option E: UAC The correct answer is Option E.
results.best_explanation: AUG = methionine  The complementary tRNA molecule would have an anticodon that pairs with the codon for methionine (AUG) and this is UAC.  The tRNA molecule carrying methionine will only bind to the Aminoacyl tRNA site on the ribosome (PEP) when the complementary anticodon (UAC) pairs with the methionine codon (AUG)  The other tRNA molecules for the other amino acids will also bind to the ribosome at the same time.  Once the tRNA molecules are bound to the ribosome, the peptidyl site on the ribosome will be available to bind the tRNA molecule that carries the growing polypeptide chain.  The ribosome will then perform the peptidyl site turnover, where the Aminoacyl site tRNA molecule is ejected and replaced with a new one.  This process will continue until the full length protein is synthesised.  The Initiation complex is then ready to bind another mRNA molecule.  The ribosomes are capable of carrying out multiple translocation events simultaneously.  Therefore, one or more ribosomes may be translating different mRNA molecules at the same time.

results.best_explanation: If a child has growth hormone in excess, they will have gigantism. This is because GH causes an increase in cell number. In children, this results in tall stature. In adults, it results in acromegaly, which is characterised by excessive growth and enlargement of bones, tendons, and other tissues. This leads to severe organ enlargement and potential damage to the heart, blood vessels, and lungs. Gigantism is also a result of an excess in GH, but most commonly occurs in childhood, and is less severe than acromegaly. It leads to tall stature, but unlike acromegaly, the excess GH is not severe enough to cause significant organ enlargement. Gigantism leads to acromegaly in the majority of cases, as the excess GH in gigantism leads to organomegaly, and hence, severe health risks. results.best_explanation: This is a respiratory alkalosis secondary to a panic attack, as the patient is experiencing hyperventilation, which is increasing the CO2 output without a similar rise in pO2. results.question: Given question: During inflammation, neutrophils migrate to the site of injury. There are three steps to neutrophil migration: Rolling, Adhesion and Transmigration. results.best_explanation:
Selectins are carbohydrate-based molecules which are expressed on the neutrophil and endothelial cell surfaces. They allow the neutrophil to roll along the endothelium, taking up the slack vessel (it doesn't actually "roll" along the endothelium, it's just being pushed through). Integrins are the actual adhesion molecules which are expressed on the neutrophil and endothelial cell surfaces. When a neutrophil comes into contact with an endothelial cell, integrins interact, allowing the neutrophil to adhere to the endothelium. PECAM-1 (platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule 1) is an integrin which is expressed on the neutrophil and endothelial cell surfaces. It is not specifically involved in the rolling phase. Fibrin is a protein which is laid down in the clot, forming a mesh-like structure. It is not involved in the migration of neutrophils.
